title: Everyday documents: memos, labels, schedules, indexes, tables of contents
blurb: Read memos, nutrition and drug labels, schedules, indexes and tables of contents the way their layout intends.
question: A granola label lists 240 calories for a serving of 2/3 cup and about 6 servings per container. A student eats 1 1/3 cups. One answer choice says 240 calories. Why is that wrong, and what is the right total?

teach.body: Formally, everyday or functional documents are practical texts (memos, emails, labels, nutrition facts, schedules, indexes, tables of contents, forms) whose layout tells you where each kind of information lives. In plain English: each document is a map with a legend. Once you know the conventions, such as 'nutrition values are per serving' or 'an index is alphabetical', you can find anything in seconds, and you avoid the traps built on misreading the layout.

teach.caption: An appendix holds extra material; a bibliography or reference list names the sources used.

teach.body:
TO: All 3 West nursing staff
FROM: Dana Whitfield, Nurse Manager
DATE: March 3
SUBJECT: Badge reader replacement

The badge readers on 3 West will be replaced on Thursday, March 6, between 1:00 and 3:00 a.m. During that window, enter the unit using the keypad code posted at the nurses' station. Readers will work normally from 3:00 a.m.

The heading lines answer who, from whom, when written and what about. The DATE line is when the memo was written, not when the event happens.

head: Line
Value
teach.caption: Every amount and % Daily Value on the label is for ONE serving.

teach.body: Nutrition facts give amounts per serving. To find what someone actually ate, divide the amount eaten by the serving size, then multiply. Eating 1 1/3 cups of the granola is 2 servings (1 1/3 ÷ 2/3 = 2), so 2 × 240 = 480 calories. The whole container is about 6 servings: about 1,440 calories. The % Daily Value works the same way: 7% per serving becomes 14% for two servings.

teach.h: Parts of an over-the-counter drug label

children.label: Active ingredient
children.sub: What it is, amount per tablet

teach.caption: Also check the expiration date and any 'ask a doctor' line for a particular age group.
Find the row (day) and the column (provider) before reading the cell. Check a.m. and p.m.

items: Name the document type and recall its conventions (index = alphabetical; label = per serving).
Read the headings, column labels and row labels first.
Find the one row, column or section the question needs.
Check units and qualifiers: per serving, a.m. or p.m., weekday or weekend, age group.
Calculate only if the question asks (servings eaten, total cost).

teach.text: The document traps: per-serving vs per-container amounts; the memo's DATE line mistaken for the event date; a related but different index entry ('type 1' when the question says 'type 2'); the table of contents and index purposes swapped; and a value read from the neighboring row or column of a schedule.

teach.body: Brianna Lopez, applying to an LPN program, needs every page on type 2 diabetes in a health textbook. The table of contents shows only a chapter called 'Endocrine Disorders', so she turns to the index. Under 'Diabetes' she finds 'gestational, 212', 'type 1, 198-203' and 'type 2, 204-211, 340'. She reads pages 204 to 211 and page 340, and skips the type 1 pages next door.

items: Table of contents: front, page order, chapters. Index: back, alphabetical, every page for a topic. Glossary: definitions.
Memos: TO, FROM, DATE, SUBJECT. The DATE line is when it was written.
Nutrition facts are per serving; multiply by servings eaten.
Drug labels: active ingredient, uses, warnings, directions by age, expiration date.
Schedules: match row, column, day and a.m. or p.m. before reading the cell.

summary: You can now read memos, nutrition and drug labels, schedules, indexes and tables of contents by their conventions, and locate or apply the exact detail asked for. You can also avoid the per-serving, memo-date and wrong-row traps.

A.q: A student wants to find every page in a pharmacology textbook that mentions insulin. Which part of the book should she use?
options: The index at the back of the book
The table of contents at the front
The glossary at the back of the book
The reference list after each chapter
A.why: An index lists specific topics alphabetically with every page on which each appears, so it shows all the pages that mention insulin.

whyNot.1: The table of contents lists chapters and their starting pages, not every page where a topic appears.
whyNot.2: A glossary defines terms; it does not list the pages where they appear.
whyNot.3: A reference list names the sources the authors used.

A.q:
Read the label.

Nutrition Facts
Serving size: 1 cup (240 mL)
Servings per container: 2
Calories: 110
Sodium: 480 mg (21% Daily Value)
Total sugars: 6 g

Lena drinks the entire container of soup. How much sodium does she consume?
A.why: The label gives 480 mg per serving, and the container holds 2 servings: 2 × 480 mg = 960 mg.

whyNot.0: 240 is the serving size in milliliters, not the sodium.
whyNot.1: 480 mg is one serving; she drank both servings.
whyNot.3: This multiplies by 3 servings, but the container holds 2.

A.q:
Read the memo.

TO: All 3 West nursing staff
FROM: Dana Whitfield, Nurse Manager
DATE: March 3
SUBJECT: Badge reader replacement

The badge readers on 3 West will be replaced on Thursday, March 6, between 1:00 and 3:00 a.m. During that window, enter the unit using the keypad code posted at the nurses' station. Readers will work normally from 3:00 a.m.

According to the memo, when will staff need to use the keypad code?
A.why: The body says the readers are replaced on Thursday, March 6, between 1:00 and 3:00 a.m., and the keypad code is used during that window.

whyNot.0: March 3 is the date the memo was written, not the date of the work.
whyNot.1: The work is from 1:00 to 3:00 a.m., not p.m.
whyNot.2: From 3:00 a.m. the readers work normally, so the code is not needed.

B.q:
Read the index excerpt.

Diabetes
   gestational, 212
   type 1, 198-203
   type 2, 204-211, 340
Diet. See Nutrition
Digestion, 150-162

On which pages would a reader find information about type 2 diabetes?
B.why: The subentry 'type 2' under 'Diabetes' lists pages 204 to 211 and page 340.

whyNot.0: Pages 198 to 203 are listed for type 1 diabetes, the entry just above.
whyNot.1: Page 212 is for gestational diabetes, and this range leaves out page 340.
whyNot.2: This leaves out page 340, which the type 2 entry also lists.

B.q:
Read the schedule.

Clinic hours
Monday: Dr. Lee 8 a.m.-12 p.m.; NP Ortiz 1-5 p.m.
Tuesday: Dr. Lee 1-5 p.m.; NP Ortiz 8 a.m.-12 p.m.
Wednesday: Dr. Lee closed; NP Ortiz 8 a.m.-5 p.m.
Thursday: Dr. Lee 8 a.m.-5 p.m.; NP Ortiz closed

A patient who can come in the afternoon but not the morning wants to see Dr. Lee. On which days is that possible?
B.why: Dr. Lee works afternoons on Tuesday (1-5 p.m.) and Thursday (8 a.m.-5 p.m. includes the afternoon). Monday is mornings only, and Wednesday is closed.

whyNot.0: Dr. Lee's Monday hours end at 12 p.m., so there is no afternoon slot.
whyNot.1: Monday is a morning-only day for Dr. Lee.
whyNot.2: Dr. Lee is closed on Wednesday; NP Ortiz is the provider that day.

B.q:
Read the label.

Drug Facts
Active ingredient (in each tablet): antihistamine, 10 mg
Uses: temporarily relieves sneezing and runny nose due to hay fever
Directions: Adults and children 6 years and over: 1 tablet daily. Do not take more than 1 tablet in 24 hours. Children under 6 years: ask a doctor.
Expiration: 08/2027

According to the label, what should the parent of a 4-year-old do before giving this product?
options: Give half of a tablet daily
B.why: The directions say that for children under 6 years, the parent should ask a doctor. A 4-year-old is under 6.

whyNot.1: The label says nothing about taking the tablet with food, and the child is in the 'ask a doctor' group.
whyNot.2: No half-tablet dose appears on the label; this relies on outside guessing.
whyNot.3: One tablet daily is the dose for adults and children 6 and over.

C.q:
Read the label.

Nutrition Facts
Serving size: 2/3 cup (55 g)
Servings per container: about 6
Calories: 240
Total fat: 9 g (12% Daily Value)
Sodium: 150 mg (7% Daily Value)

Jordan eats 1 1/3 cups of the granola. According to the label, how many calories does he consume?
C.why: 1 1/3 cups is two servings of 2/3 cup (2/3 + 2/3 = 4/3 = 1 1/3). Two servings × 240 calories = 480 calories.

whyNot.0: 240 calories is one serving; he ate two.
whyNot.1: This multiplies 240 by 1 1/3 cups, treating the serving as 1 cup instead of 2/3 cup.
whyNot.3: 1,440 is roughly the whole container (6 servings), not what he ate.

C.q:
Read the table of contents.

Contents
1 Cells and Tissues ..... 1
2 The Skeletal System ..... 27
3 The Muscular System ..... 58
4 The Nervous System ..... 85
5 The Endocrine System ..... 121

On which pages is the chapter on the muscular system?
C.why: A table of contents gives starting pages. Chapter 3 starts on page 58, and Chapter 4 starts on page 85, so Chapter 3 runs from 58 to 84.

whyNot.0: Pages 27 to 57 are Chapter 2, the skeletal system.
whyNot.2: This runs into Chapter 4, which begins on page 85.
whyNot.3: Pages 85 to 120 are Chapter 4, the nervous system.

C.q:
Read the email.

From: Human Resources
To: All new hires
Subject: Action needed before your start date

Please bring your immunization records to Room 110 any weekday between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. before your start date. If you have already uploaded your records online, you need to bring a photo ID to Room 110 instead.

Sam uploaded his immunization records online last week. According to the email, what must he do?
options: Bring his immunization records to Room 110
Bring a photo ID to Room 110 on a weekday
Upload his records online again before starting
Wait for HR to email him an appointment time
C.why: Sam has already uploaded his records, so the second sentence applies: he brings a photo ID to Room 110, on a weekday between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m.

whyNot.0: Bringing the records is for new hires who have not uploaded them.
whyNot.2: The email never asks anyone to upload records twice.
whyNot.3: The email gives drop-in hours; it says nothing about HR sending appointment times.

reteach.title: A grocery store has a layout
reteach.question: In a grocery store you never search every shelf for milk; you read the aisle signs. How is reading an everyday document the same?

blocks.h: Signs tell you where to look
blocks.body: Aisle signs are the headings. The store directory by the door is like a table of contents: sections in order. A list of every product with its aisle number would be an index. The price tag on the shelf says '$3.99 per pound', and if you buy 2 pounds you pay twice that: exactly like 'per serving' on a nutrition label. Read the sign, find the shelf, check the unit.

blocks.text: A price per pound is not the price of the whole bag, and a label's calories per serving are not the calories in the whole box.

explain.body: Table of contents: front, chapters in page order with starting pages. Index: back, alphabetical topics with every page. Glossary: alphabetical definitions of key terms.

head: Task
Use
rows: See how a book is organized
Find every page on a topic
Look up what a term means

test.q: While reading a biology textbook, a student meets the term 'osmosis' and wants a short definition. Where should she look first?
test.why: A glossary gives alphabetical definitions of key terms used in the book.

whyNot.1: The index lists the pages where 'osmosis' appears; it does not define it.
whyNot.2: The table of contents lists chapters and starting pages.
whyNot.3: A bibliography lists the sources the authors used.

explain.body: Every amount and % Daily Value on a nutrition label is for one serving. Servings eaten = amount eaten ÷ serving size. Total = per serving × servings eaten.

test.q: A snack label says: serving size 15 chips; servings per container 4; calories 160; total fat 10 g. Malik eats 30 chips. How much fat does he eat?
test.why: 30 chips ÷ 15 chips per serving = 2 servings. 2 × 10 g = 20 g of fat.

whyNot.0: 10 g is the fat in one serving of 15 chips.
whyNot.2: This multiplies by 3 servings; 30 chips is 2 servings.
whyNot.3: 40 g is the fat in the whole container of 4 servings.

explain.body: Find the row and the column first, then read the cell. Check the day type (weekday or weekend) and a.m. or p.m.

test.q: A hospital shuttle runs weekdays from 6:00 a.m. to 9:30 p.m., every 15 minutes, and weekends from 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., every 30 minutes. What time does the last shuttle run on a Sunday?
test.why: Sunday is a weekend day, and the weekend shuttle runs until 6:00 p.m.

whyNot.0: 6:00 a.m. is the first weekday shuttle.
whyNot.1: 8:00 a.m. is the first weekend shuttle, not the last.
whyNot.3: 9:30 p.m. is the last weekday shuttle.

explain.body: TO = audience, FROM = sender, DATE = when it was written, SUBJECT = topic. The event date and the action needed are in the body.

test.q: A memo reads: 'TO: Pharmacy technicians / FROM: Lisa Grant, Pharmacy Director / DATE: June 2 / SUBJECT: Inventory count. Inventory will be counted on June 14 after closing. All technicians scheduled that day should stay one extra hour.' Who is expected to act on this memo?
options: Lisa Grant and the pharmacy's managers
Every technician who works on June 2
test.why: The memo is addressed to pharmacy technicians, and the body asks technicians scheduled on the count day, June 14, to stay an extra hour.

whyNot.0: The TO line names technicians, not all pharmacy staff.
whyNot.2: Lisa Grant is the sender (FROM), not the audience.
whyNot.3: June 2 is the memo date; the count is on June 14.
